lead: Flexural design is a set of checks at two moments in a member's life. At transfer the full initial prestress meets young concrete and only the self-weight resists it; at service the prestress has dropped by its losses and the full load acts. The fibre stresses at both stages must stay inside the code limits, and the section must also have enough ultimate moment, when the tendon stress rises far above the effective prestress.
prereq: You need the stress concept, the loss ratio η = Pe/Pi, and the limit state stress block 0.36 fck b xu with lever arm d − 0.42 xu.

blocks.text: Let f<sub>ct</sub> and f<sub>tt</sub> be the permissible compression and tension at transfer, and f<sub>cw</sub> and f<sub>tw</sub> those at service (all as positive numbers). For a beam with the tendon below the centroid, the four conditions at the critical section are:

Transfer, top:   P<sub>i</sub>/A − P<sub>i</sub>e/Z<sub>t</sub> + M<sub>g</sub>/Z<sub>t</sub> ≥ −f<sub>tt</sub>
Transfer, bottom: P<sub>i</sub>/A + P<sub>i</sub>e/Z<sub>b</sub> − M<sub>g</sub>/Z<sub>b</sub> ≤ f<sub>ct</sub>
Service, top:    P<sub>e</sub>/A − P<sub>e</sub>e/Z<sub>t</sub> + M<sub>t</sub>/Z<sub>t</sub> ≤ f<sub>cw</sub>
Service, bottom:  P<sub>e</sub>/A + P<sub>e</sub>e/Z<sub>b</sub> − M<sub>t</sub>/Z<sub>b</sub> ≥ −f<sub>tw</sub>
blocks.where: M<sub>g</sub> is the self-weight moment, M<sub>t</sub> = M<sub>g</sub> + M<sub>q</sub> the total service moment and M<sub>q</sub> the live-load moment, in N·mm. Exam questions usually give the permissible stresses.

blocks.text: The tension limit at service depends on the type of member in IS 1343. Type 1: no tensile stress at service (liquid-retaining structures, severe exposure). Type 2: tension allowed but below the cracking stress, so no visible cracks. Type 3: cracks allowed, with the width limited, which is partial prestressing. Some syllabi write Class 1, 2 and 3 for the same idea.

sections.h3: Choosing the section and the eccentricity

blocks.text: Combining the transfer and service conditions at each fibre eliminates P and e and gives the smallest section moduli that can work:

Z<sub>t</sub> ≥ (M<sub>q</sub> + (1 − η)M<sub>g</sub>)/(f<sub>cw</sub> + η f<sub>tt</sub>)
Z<sub>b</sub> ≥ (M<sub>q</sub> + (1 − η)M<sub>g</sub>)/(η f<sub>ct</sub> + f<sub>tw</sub>)
blocks.where: η is the loss ratio P<sub>e</sub>/P<sub>i</sub>, often 0.8 to 0.85; the other symbols are as above. The live-load moment, not the dead load, drives the section size, because the dead load is present at transfer to cancel part of the prestress.

blocks.text: With a section chosen, the transfer-top condition gives the largest eccentricity and the service-bottom condition the smallest. Plotting all four conditions as lines of 1/P against e is Magnel's graphical method.

At collapse the bonded tendon strains with the cracked concrete around it, so its stress rises from the effective value (about 0.6 f<sub>pu</sub>) towards its strength. The tendon strain is the effective prestrain plus the strain of the concrete at tendon level: ε<sub>p</sub> = f<sub>pe</sub>/E<sub>s</sub> + 0.0035(d − x<sub>u</sub>)/x<sub>u</sub>. When that strain is well past the elastic range, the tendon reaches its design stress f<sub>pb</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>p</sub>. With the limit state stress block of IS 456:
0.36 f<sub>ck</sub> b x<sub>u</sub> = f<sub>pb</sub> A<sub>p</sub>,   M<sub>u</sub> = f<sub>pb</sub> A<sub>p</sub>(d − 0.42 x<sub>u</sub>)
blocks.where: f<sub>ck</sub> in N/mm²; b the width and d the depth to the tendon centroid in mm; A<sub>p</sub> in mm²; M<sub>u</sub> in N·mm. IS 1343 also gives a table of f<sub>pb</sub>/0.87f<sub>p</sub> and x<sub>u</sub>/d against A<sub>p</sub>f<sub>p</sub>/(b d f<sub>ck</sub>) for rectangular sections, which reduces f<sub>pb</sub> when that ratio is large.

blocks.text: Flanged sections are treated as reinforced T-beams. Compare M<sub>u</sub> with the factored moment 1.5(M<sub>g</sub> + M<sub>q</sub>).

examples.question: A pre-tensioned beam 300 mm × 800 mm spans 12 m and carries a live load of 12 kN/m besides its self-weight (25 kN/m³). P<sub>i</sub> = 1500 kN and η = 0.8. Permissible stresses: at transfer 16 N/mm² compression and 1.4 N/mm² tension; at service 15 N/mm² compression and no tension (Type 1). Check the midspan section with e = 250 mm, then with e = 220 mm, and find the range of eccentricity that works.
steps: e = 250 mm, transfer: P<sub>i</sub>/A = 6.25, P<sub>i</sub>e/Z = 11.72, M<sub>g</sub>/Z = 3.375. Top = −2.09 N/mm²: 2.09 N/mm² tension exceeds 1.4, so this fails. Bottom = 14.59 N/mm² ≤ 16, safe.
e = 220 mm, transfer: P<sub>i</sub>e/Z = 10.312. Top = 6.25 − 10.312 + 3.375 = −0.688 N/mm² (tension 0.69 ≤ 1.4, safe); bottom = 13.188 N/mm² ≤ 16, safe.
e = 220 mm, service: P<sub>e</sub>/A = 5, P<sub>e</sub>e/Z = 8.25, M<sub>t</sub>/Z = 10.125. Top = 6.875 N/mm² ≤ 15, safe; bottom = 3.125 N/mm², compression, so no tension: Type 1 met.
Largest e from the transfer-top condition: e ≤ (P<sub>i</sub>/A + M<sub>g</sub>/Z + 1.4)Z/P<sub>i</sub> = (6.25 + 3.375 + 1.4) × 32 × 10⁶/1,500,000 = 235.2 mm.
Smallest e from the service-bottom condition: P<sub>e</sub>/A + P<sub>e</sub>e/Z ≥ M<sub>t</sub>/Z gives e ≥ (10.125 − 5) × 32 × 10⁶/1,200,000 = 136.7 mm.
examples.answer: With e = 250 mm the top fibre has 2.09 N/mm² tension at transfer, more than the 1.4 allowed. With e = 220 mm all four checks pass (transfer −0.69 and 13.19, service 6.88 and 3.12 N/mm²). Any e from 137 to 235 mm works.

examples.question: A pre-tensioned beam 250 mm wide with d = 500 mm (D = 600 mm) of M40 concrete has three 12.7 mm strands (98.7 mm² each, f<sub>p</sub> = 1860 N/mm²) with an effective stress of 1116 N/mm². Find M<sub>u</sub> and check it for a span of 8 m with a live load of 10 kN/m.
steps: Strain check: ε<sub>p</sub> = 1116/195,000 + 0.0035 × (366.9/133.1) = 0.00572 + 0.00965 = 0.0154, far beyond the elastic range (about 0.007), so f<sub>pb</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>p</sub> holds.
Factored moment: self-weight 0.25 × 0.6 × 25 = 3.75 kN/m; 1.5 × (3.75 + 10) × 8²/8 = 165 kN·m ≤ 212.8 kN·m, safe.
examples.answer: M<sub>u</sub> = 212.8 kN·m against a factored moment of 165 kN·m, a margin of 1.29; the tendon yields well before the concrete crushes, so the failure is ductile.

traps: Using P<sub>e</sub>/A<sub>p</sub> as the tendon stress at ultimate. At collapse a bonded tendon reaches f<sub>pb</sub>, near 0.87 f<sub>p</sub>.
Leaving the self-weight out of the transfer check. It is present at transfer and is what allows a large eccentricity.
Checking transfer with P<sub>e</sub> or service with P<sub>i</sub>. Transfer uses P<sub>i</sub> and M<sub>g</sub>; service uses P<sub>e</sub> and M<sub>t</sub>.
Writing tension limits with the wrong sign. Keep compression positive and write each tension condition as f ≥ −f<sub>t</sub>.
Unit slips: N/mm² × mm³ gives N·mm; divide by 10⁶ for kN·m.

quiz.q: What are Type 1, Type 2 and Type 3 prestressed members?
quiz.a: Type 1: no tension at service. Type 2: tension below the cracking stress, no visible cracks. Type 3: cracking allowed with limited crack width (partially prestressed).

quiz.q: Why does the live-load moment, and not the dead-load moment, set the minimum section modulus?
quiz.a: The dead load acts at transfer as well as at service, so it is resisted by choosing a larger eccentricity; only the moment that appears after transfer, M<sub>q</sub> plus the part (1 − η)M<sub>g</sub> released by the losses, must be carried by the section's stress range.

quiz.q: For the first worked example, find the service stresses with e = 200 mm and say whether Type 1 is met.

A bonded rectangular section has b = 300 mm, d = 600 mm, A<sub>p</sub> = 400 mm², f<sub>p</sub> = 1860 N/mm² and M45 concrete. Taking f<sub>pb</sub> = 0.87 f<sub>p</sub>, find x<sub>u</sub> and M<sub>u</sub>.
A Type 2 member shows a calculated service tension of 4.2 N/mm² while its modulus of rupture is 3.5 N/mm². What do you conclude, and what are the options?
quiz.a: The section will crack, so it is not Type 2. Increase the prestress or the eccentricity within the transfer limits, enlarge the section, or design it as Type 3 with untensioned bars to control the crack width.

beyond: Not for the exam. Design offices check every section along the span, not only midspan. For unbonded and external tendons the stress at collapse rises much less, because the tendon strain is spread over its whole length; codes give separate formulas. Search for Magnel diagram, unbonded tendon stress at ultimate and IS 1343 limit state of collapse.
